roadmap.goal: A system administrator finds every instance-wide switch in one table - including the one that decides who owns the forecast order - and turning that one on moves nobody. The ordering choice stops being an AppSetting behind its own section and becomes an OptionalFeature row written through a per-key applier that seeds the places before it flips the value; the write is addressed by the key the store actually keys these rows by; and the table resolves terminology tokens in a row's name as well as its description, so the seeded string reads in the instance's own word.

validation.notes: Pass 1 returned REJECT with 3 blockers and 3 majors. Five did not survive checking against the code and were rejected with evidence: the orphaned-scenario count was wrong (14 of 15 RED were already traceable); sabotage instructions did exist, in 02-03, 02-04, 02-05 and 02-07; the ordering-constraint blocker was self-refuting, having verified deps 02-01 as correct in its own text; and all three majors were filed as verification needed rather than performed. Those three were then performed: SetPolicy has exactly one production caller (AppSettingService.cs:108) and one test touchpoint (AppSettingServiceTest.cs:37,52), FeatureOrderingPolicyProvider is its only implementor and every other reference is a Moq mock, so deletion is safe; obligation 6 is genuinely discharged by useFeatureOrdering.test.tsx:60,68,100 plus FeatureListDataGrid.test.tsx:14; and AppSettingService.cs:103 does guard the seed on ManualOrder, so the roadmap follows the code rather than the ADR C4 diagram. Pass 1 did half-find one real orphan. Three defects were fixed before pass 2: the frontend scenario leaves no separate section behind was named nowhere in the JSON; 02-08 and 02-09 misused scenario_name (a PNG path, and a scenario 02-04 owns); and the seeded name and description were pinned by no test at all, since the frontend suite is mock-driven and only the key is checked by running the suites - 02-02 now owes a literal-text probe in OptionalFeatureSeederTests. Pass 2 returned no blockers, confirmed the three vacuous-pass claims hold with no unmarked fourth, and confirmed 02-02 scenarios survive the store moving under them at 02-05 because AssertTheOrderingSettingReads reads the table directly rather than through the policy port. Its one finding - a step saying a scenario goes green here without telling the crafter to remove the skip marker - was general rather than local: only 02-04 carried an explicit directive and no step carried one for the frontend it.skip markers at all. Every claiming step now names the markers it removes. Baselines at approval: backend 6343 passed / 0 failed / 11 skipped, frontend 4639 passed / 4 skipped, the skips being exactly this slice RED scaffolds.

out_of_scope: Renaming the OptionalFeature entity, its table or its route prefix. The row joins a table that already exists under the name it already has; the group heading above it changes and nothing beneath it does. Renaming the entity would be an EF migration on four providers plus a client-side model rename, for a word

Deleting the AppSetting row FeatureOrdering:Policy or either alias endpoint. Additive only - a migration that turns out to have been wrong has no way back once the row it read is gone, and the aliases are what keep an older client working. OQ-4 puts their removal at the next contract drop, which is a later release's decision and not this slice's

Any change to what manual ordering does. Move actions, the position column's behaviour, Features shared across Portfolios and ADO #5691 are all Epic #5375's, shipped and unchanged. This slice moves the switch that turns ordering on; it does not touch a single line of what happens after it is on

Any change to DeltaSync beyond the heading above it. It is not premium and must not become gated, its name carries no terminology token, and its stored on/off, preview badge, name and description are all somebody else's decision. The_setting_that_was_already_in_the_list_is_carried_across_untouched compares all five and is carried as a regression criterion on every backend step

Making the premium gate a product-wide concept. The refusal is symmetric - a disable is refused on the same terms as an enable - and that is settled (ADR-187 section 6, DDD-14, UI-8). The coherent version, letting an instance relinquish premium configuration across ordering, blackout periods and recurring rules alike, is a product-wide change that belongs on the board as its own item. Nothing in this slice makes the branch direction-sensitive

Per-key configuration richer than a boolean. IOptionalFeatureApplier takes the row and the new on/off value; it does not gain options, a payload or a settings blob. A third ordering policy would need a new store rather than a new enum member, which is the accepted residual recorded in ADR-187's consequences

An EF migration. There is none. The value move is a seeder step between two tables that both already exist, and OptionalFeature.Id keeps its column and its place on the wire - it simply stops naming a row. Any step that finds itself reaching for the CreateMigration script has misread the design and should stop

Widening ApiHelpers.GetEntityByIdAnExecuteAction. Rejected in slice 01 on blast radius - 83 call sites across 8 controllers, no other beneficiary. This action already stopped using it; slice 02 retires the route that was the last place the numeric identity survived, and leaves the helper untouched

Keyed DI as a project idiom. OQ-2 is decided in favour of a dictionary built from the registered appliers (see 02-04), which is a decision about this one seam. Nothing here proposes AddKeyedScoped anywhere else, and no existing registration is rewritten
AC-02.5 is not a step. Re-reading Epic #5733's delta and slice 03 to confirm neither still claims the refusal is a document check, done by reading, and it belongs to finalization

phases.name: One list of switches
phases.description: The ordering choice moves into the behaviour-settings table: addressed by key on both stacks, seeded with the value the instance already chose, written through an applier that seeds the places before it flips the value, read from one store behind both doors, and rendered in the instance's own word under one heading.

steps.name: The toggle names the setting the way the store does
steps.scenario_name: switches one setting without touching the other
criteria: POST api/v1/OptionalFeatures/{featureKey} and POST api/latest/OptionalFeatures/{featureKey} resolve the row through the setting's key, and no route on this controller addresses an OptionalFeature by a number any more

A toggle aimed at a key nobody seeded answers 404, and it does so from the lookup rather than from a premium check hoisted above it - the request claims to be premium and must still be told the setting does not exist

Two settings rendered in the table are switched one at a time: clicking Faster Updates leaves the ordering switch exactly as it was, on a page where both rows carry the identity the seeder really writes

The client posts to /optionalfeatures/{key}, keys its rows on the setting's key in both places the table keys them, and matches its optimistic update on the key - so no click can move a row it was not aimed at and React sees no duplicate key
GET /OptionalFeatures/{featureKey} answers with the setting a caller names and not merely with some setting, asserted against the real repository rather than against a mocked predicate
Every scenario in Slice01PremiumRefusalTest is still green, including the refusal, its wording, the two-door comparison and the not-found guard
Both DeltaSync licence states are still taken - the non-premium setting is switched on a licensed and on an unlicensed instance alike
No scenario's Given, When or Then changed. The harness posts a key where it used to post a number; what the scenarios say is untouched
steps.implementation_notes: THIS STEP MUST LAND BEFORE 02-02, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON IT IS FIRST. LighthouseAppContext.cs:102 keys OptionalFeature by its string Key, so Id is an ordinary mapped column with nothing generating it and the seeder writes every row zero. RepositoryBase.GetById is a SingleOrDefault on Id. Today there is exactly one seeded row, so the numeric route happens to work; 02-02 adds the second, and from that instant GetById(0) matches two rows and throws for BOTH settings - including DeltaSync, which this story promised not to touch. Do this after the seeder and a committed green test (The_setting_the_licence_has_nothing_to_say_about_is_taken_either_way, which toggles DeltaSync) goes red mid-slice for an addressing reason, which is exactly the failure that gets fixed in the test instead of in the product. BACKEND: change the action to [HttpPost("{featureKey}")] public async Task<ActionResult<OptionalFeature>> UpdateOptionalFeature(string featureKey, [FromBody] OptionalFeature updatedFeature) and resolve with repository.GetByPredicate(f => f.Key == featureKey) - the same shape the shipped GET on line 25 already uses. Keep the order of operations slice 01 pinned: lookup, then NotFound, then the premium 403, then set Enabled, Update, Save, Ok(feature). Keep [RbacGuard(RbacGuardRequirement.SystemAdmin)] - a test reads it reflectively. Remove the numeric route outright: no [HttpPost("{id:int}")] alias. An alias would keep GetById(0) alive, which is the one lookup that throws once 02-02 lands, so what it offers a caller is a 500 (ADR-187 alternative F). THE HARNESS FOLLOWS ITS PORT, and that is a stated consequence rather than a quiet edit: ToggleOptionalFeature keeps its (key, enabled) signature, keeps the Found guard with its message, drops the id lookup and the identity-count guard, sends the whole row as raw JSON with the id field left as whatever the store holds, and posts /api/latest/optionalfeatures/{key}. IdOfStoredSetting and CountOfSettingsCarryingIdentity become dead scaffolding and go with it - a private helper left behind that nothing calls is an unused-member finding waiting to happen and, worse, reads as a guard that is still guarding. ToggleASettingThatDoesNotExist aims at a key nobody can name rather than at 987654 and keeps its isPremium true body, because that body is what catches a premium check hoisted above the lookup whether the hoist reads the request or the store. THE UNIT TEST STOPS COMPILING, and that is the point: OptionalFeaturesControllerTest calls UpdateOptionalFeature(1, feature) and (0, feature) directly and mocks GetById. Move those calls to a key, mock GetByPredicate (its parameter is Func<OptionalFeature,bool>), and rename the two methods whose names say FeatureWithId - they name an identity that no longer exists. Slice 01 already extends this class, so this is a rename inside work already in hand. THE UNCOVERED PREDICATE, AND WHY THIS STEP OWNS IT: slice 01's mutation run recorded OptionalFeaturesController.cs:25 - f.Key == featureKey inside GetOptionalFeatureByKey - as NoCoverage. The unit tests mock GetByPredicate, so Moq hands back a canned row without ever invoking the lambda, and no scenario reads a setting by key. This step routes the WRITE through exactly that predicate shape, and 02-06 makes the client's ordering read depend on the READ one, so an uncovered equality becomes load-bearing twice over. Add one acceptance scenario to Slice02OneListOfSwitchesScenarios.cs - The_setting_a_caller_names_is_the_setting_it_gets_back - with a harness helper mirroring GetOptionalFeatures, asserting that reading DeltaSync by its key returns DeltaSync's name and premium flag and that a key nobody seeded answers 404. It is a NEW test authored in DELIVER rather than a DISTILL scenario, and that is acceptable here for the reason ci-learnings already names: mutation-driven test-strengthening is where survivors get closed, the suite already runs against the real repository through WebApplicationFactory so the cost is one helper and one method, and inverting that comparison must not be a change the suite can sleep through. FRONTEND, SAME COMMIT, because routing the server by key does not fix the browser and a server that has moved while the client has not is a broken toggle on trunk: OptionalFeatureService.updateFeature posts to /optionalfeatures/ plus feature.key - getFeatureByKey is already the shape to copy; SystemSettingsTab.tsx keys the LicenseTooltip wrapper AND the TableRow inside it on feature.key, and matches its optimistic update on feature.key rather than feature.id. All four, or the twin survives. GATES: dotnet build with zero warnings (TreatWarningsAsErrors makes any warning a failure); dotnet test --filter "TestCategory!=Integration&TestCategory!=JiraIntegration&TestCategory!=LinearIntegration&TestCategory!=AdoIntegration&TestCategory!=ServiceNowIntegration"; pnpm test; pnpm build; pnpm biome check ./src. CI-LEARNINGS THAT BITE HERE: CA1859 - the new harness helper and any local holding a row take the concrete type, never IRepository or an interface; NUnit2045 - the new scenario's two assertions go inside using (Assert.EnterMultipleScope()), and the analyser does not see through a private helper, so a helper with two Assert.That calls needs the scope inside it; NUnit1028 - anything in the fixture that is not a Test or TestCase method is private static; CA1861 - no inline array literal in an assertion, hoist to a static readonly field; S1192 - the key literal now appears in several places in the harness, so give it a const before the third occurrence rather than after CI says so. COMMIT: two, both conventional - fix(optional-features) for the route and its client, test(optional-features) for the harness and unit-test adaptation. COMMENTS: the harness constant FeatureOrderingOptionalFeatureKey keeps its literal FeatureOrdering - do NOT repoint it at the production constant when 02-02 creates one, because the frontend suite names the same literal and the key is the wire identity the browser addresses the row by, so a rename that both suites accept would break the page; its comment is rewritten to say that reason instead of the expired one about compiling against a constant that did not exist. No comment anywhere in this step may cite UI-1, DDD-13, ADR-187 section 8 or AC-01.1 - those name documents a cold reader cannot open. Write the reason itself.  UN-SKIP / UN-IGNORE, EXPLICITLY: remove the it.skip from switches one setting without touching the other in SystemSettingsTab.behaviourSettings.test.tsx. The new by-key read scenario this step authors is written without a skip marker from the start. The committed suite ships green - every scaffold carries a skip marker and DELIVER removes them one at a time. A step that implements the behaviour but leaves the marker in place turns nothing green and the suite still passes, which is indistinguishable from delivered work. Remove the marker, watch it fail, then make it pass.

steps.name: The ordering setting joins the table, carrying what the instance already chose
criteria: The behaviour-settings table holds a row for the ordering choice, marked premium, off by default, named and described for what it does rather than for the mechanism behind it
An instance that already owned its order comes out of the upgrade still owning it, with every place it had chosen byte-identical

An instance that left the order with its tracker does not acquire it in the upgrade - and neither does one that never had the setting at all, nor one whose stored value is a word the product does not recognise
The setting the upgrade read is still stored afterwards. Nothing deletes it
The two settings in the table are switched one at a time, and switching the ordering one leaves Faster Updates exactly as it was in all five of the things that are somebody else's decision
Re-running the seeders never overwrites a stored on/off, so an instance that has switched the setting since its upgrade keeps its own answer
The seeded name and description carry terminology tokens, stored verbatim - the server resolves nothing
The seeded name and description are pinned against their literal text by a test, so a change to the words an administrator reads cannot pass unnoticed
steps.implementation_notes: THE HIGHEST-CONSEQUENCE CODE IN THE STORY, and it gets exactly one attempt per instance. AddOrUpdateCurrentFeatures refreshes Name, Description, IsPreview and IsPremium on a key it already knows and NEVER touches Enabled - deliberately, because whether a setting is on is the operator's answer and not ours. So the only place the value migration can run is the first-add branch, if (existing == null), and a release that migrates wrongly cannot be repaired by a later seed. Read the AppSetting row FeatureOrderingPolicy there, and seed Enabled true only where its value reads exactly ManualOrder. Anything else - SourceOrder, an absent row, a word nobody recognises, an empty string - seeds off, which is the same default an absent row has always meant. Do not parse leniently and do not fall back to on when surprised; the three-case TestCase in An_instance_that_never_took_its_order_over_does_not_acquire_it_in_the_upgrade exists precisely because a migration that always seeds on would satisfy the ManualOrder case on its own. Keep the read narrow: this is a seeder, so go through the context the seeder already holds rather than injecting a repository, and read only the value. THE KEY: OptionalFeatureKeys.FeatureOrderingKey with the literal FeatureOrdering, beside DeltaSyncKey. The literal must match what the harness and the frontend suite both name, and that is checked by running them, not by reading. THE COPY: the name is the label users read today, carried across from the control being deleted, with the configurable term as a token - Let Lighthouse own the order of your {{features}}. The description is the help text folded in from the same control, also tokenised. Double braces, camelCase keys from TERMINOLOGY_KEYS. The server stores the token and resolves nothing: the term map is a client-side concern and the seeding path has no principal to resolve it for. Seed IsPremium true and IsPreview false. THE COMMENT THAT MUST GO, NOT BE CORRECTED: GetOptionalFeatures carries a line claiming that zero lets EF assign the key. It is false - the entity is keyed by Key, nothing generates Id - and it is why the ambiguity survived a release, because it asserts the very behaviour a reader would otherwise have checked. Delete it outright. Once the write path is addressed by key there is no Id story left to tell, so a corrected version would be a comment about nothing. WHAT MUST NOT MOVE: the DeltaSync entry keeps its name, description, preview flag and non-premium status exactly as they are, and RemoveDeprecatedFeatures is untouched. WHAT GOES GREEN HERE AND WHY: An_instance_that_already_owned_its_order_still_owns_it_after_the_upgrade, all three cases of An_instance_that_never_took_its_order_over_does_not_acquire_it_in_the_upgrade, and Each_setting_in_the_list_is_switched_on_its_own. The last one is only reachable because 02-01 landed first - it toggles the new row through the port, which could not name either row before. The ordering policy those scenarios read still comes from the AppSetting at this point; the store is unified in 02-05 and both keep passing across it. DO NOT UN-IGNORE Turning_the_ordering_setting_on_for_the_first_time_moves_nobody, Giving_the_order_back_writes_no_places or Taking_the_order_over_again_restores_the_places_this_instance_already_chose here. All three PASS at this step and prove nothing: no seed runs, no place is ever written, so nothing moves for want of a mechanism rather than because of one. They belong to 02-04 and 02-05, where they can fail. REGRESSIONS TO WATCH, and the reason 02-01 is a dependency rather than a preference: The_setting_the_licence_has_nothing_to_say_about_is_taken_either_way toggles DeltaSync and is the test the second row would have broken; The_setting_that_was_already_in_the_list_is_carried_across_untouched compares DeltaSync's whole shape; The_upgrade_leaves_the_setting_it_migrated_from_in_place guards the AppSetting row against a tidy-up. OptionalFeatureSeederTests gains a case for the first-add migration on each stored value - it is an IntegrationTestBase fixture with the real context, which is what makes it able to say anything about a seeder. GATES: dotnet build zero warnings under TreatWarningsAsErrors; dotnet test --filter "TestCategory!=Integration&TestCategory!=JiraIntegration&TestCategory!=LinearIntegration&TestCategory!=AdoIntegration&TestCategory!=ServiceNowIntegration". CI-LEARNINGS THAT BITE HERE: S1192 - the ManualOrder literal and the new key both risk a third occurrence in one file, extract a const before writing the third; CA1859 - the private helper that reads the stored policy returns the concrete type, never IEnumerable or an interface; S125 - the replacement prose comments must not end a line in a semicolon or the analyser reads them as commented-out code and breaks the build; NUnit2045 and NUnit1028 in the seeder test as in 02-01. No EF migration is generated here or anywhere in this slice; if the model differ has something to say, something has gone wrong. COMMIT: feat(optional-features). COMMENTS: the migration branch earns one, because a stranger cannot read off the code why it may only run once - say that the seeder never overwrites a stored on/off, so this is the single moment an existing instance's choice can be carried across. Never write D1, AC-01.3, ADR-187 section 1 or UI-1 in it. THE COPY IS PINNED BY NOTHING TODAY, AND THIS STEP OWES THAT. The note above says the literal is checked by running the suites. That is true of the KEY - the acceptance harness names FeatureOrdering and would fail on a mismatch - and false of the name and the description. The frontend suite is mock-driven: it declares its own row fixture and never reads the seeder, so seeding different words leaves both stacks green while the docs, which fold this exact help text in as the rows description, quietly describe something the product does not say. Add a probe to OptionalFeatureSeederTests that asserts the seeded name and description against their literal strings, including the {{features}} tokens - the same shape The_setting_that_was_already_in_the_list_is_carried_across_untouched uses for Faster Updates. Compare against the literal, never against the constant the seeder read it from: a test that compares a value to its own source is self-satisfying and blanking the string survives it.  UN-SKIP / UN-IGNORE, EXPLICITLY: remove the [Ignore] from An_instance_that_already_owned_its_order_still_owns_it_after_the_upgrade, from An_instance_that_never_took_its_order_over_does_not_acquire_it_in_the_upgrade (all three cases move together - the attribute is on the method), and from Each_setting_in_the_list_is_switched_on_its_own. Leave every other [Ignore] in this fixture exactly where it is; the three named in the DO NOT UN-IGNORE list above belong to later steps. The committed suite ships green - every scaffold carries a skip marker and DELIVER removes them one at a time. A step that implements the behaviour but leaves the marker in place turns nothing green and the suite still passes, which is indistinguishable from delivered work. Remove the marker, watch it fail, then make it pass.

steps.name: The rank seed reads source order without asking who owns it
criteria: Seeding missing places produces the tracker's sequence even when the instance already owns the order and no Feature has a place yet - the result does not depend on when the seed runs relative to the switch
The seeder no longer asks who owns the order before deciding what sequence to seed from
The ordering seam is still the only production type that constructs a comparer - FeatureOrderingSingleSourceArchUnitTest is green and unedited
Places already chosen are never overwritten, and a Feature that arrives between the projection and the write keeps whatever place it has
Every existing consumer of the ordering seam - the Features view, the Portfolio detail, the forecast queue and the position map - reads the same sequence it read before
steps.implementation_notes: THE TEMPORAL COUPLING THIS DELETES: FeatureRankSeeder.SeedMissingRanks gets its sequence from featureOrdering.Order(orderKeys), which consults the policy. It produces source order today only because the shipped write path happens to seed before it records the choice. That is invisible at both sites, and it is the single most dangerous thing about moving this setting: seed after the flip and Order sorts by an all-null ManualRank, renumbering every Feature in row order at the exact moment the product promises nothing will move. Give IFeatureOrdering a policy-independent source-order method - OrderBySourceOrder over FeatureOrderKey - and have the seeder call it. GO THROUGH THE SEAM, NOT AROUND IT. Reaching for the source-order comparer directly from the seeder is the shorter diff and it breaks FeatureOrderingSingleSourceArchUnitTest, which exists to keep exactly one production type constructing a comparer. That test must stay green and must stay unedited; if it goes red, the fix is in the new method's location, never in the test. S4136 IS ERROR SEVERITY IN THIS REPOSITORY AND IT WILL BREAK YOUR LOCAL BUILD: all overloads of a method must be adjacent. IFeatureOrdering already carries two Order overloads. If the new method is named Order it goes directly beside them, never at the end of the interface or the class - and the rule fires in every implementing file at once, so check the test doubles too. Naming it OrderBySourceOrder sidesteps the rule and says what it does at the call site, which is the better outcome: a reader of FeatureRankSeeder should not have to know the policy exists to know what sequence the seed uses. THE TEST THIS STEP OWES is the one ADR-187 names under Architectural Enforcement and DISTILL carries as an obligation: call SeedMissingRanks with the policy already reading ManualOrder and every ManualRank null, and assert the places come out in the tracker's sequence. It is a statement about a seam rather than about a port, which is why no acceptance scenario carries it - the acceptance suite covers the consequence, this covers the cause. No FeatureRankSeeder test file exists yet, so create one following OptionalFeatureSeederTests: an IntegrationTestBase fixture with the real LighthouseAppContext, the real ordering seam, and the policy provider arranged to say ManualOrder. Fixture Features must be ranked the opposite way to their creation order or the assertion cannot fail - a fixture in row order passes whichever sequence the seeder read, which is the shape of a test that guards nothing. PROVE IT CAN FAIL before committing: point the seeder back at the policy-dependent Order and watch it go red. ci-learnings names this explicitly for any assertion whose failure you have not seen, and note that a false-guarded branch does not work in this codebase - TreatWarningsAsErrors turns unreachable code into a build error, so sabotage by substitution, not by disabling. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: the seed still fills only nulls, still appends after the highest existing place, still re-reads inside the write step so a place written concurrently is never overwritten, and still uses the narrow projection rather than the Feature repository, because writing a place back over the full Include graph re-inserts the join rows between a Portfolio and its Teams. NO ACCEPTANCE SCENARIO IS CLAIMED BY THIS STEP and that is correct: the behaviour it fixes is not observable through a port on its own. Its consequence is claimed at 02-05. GATES: dotnet build zero warnings under TreatWarningsAsErrors; dotnet test --filter "TestCategory!=Integration&TestCategory!=JiraIntegration&TestCategory!=LinearIntegration&TestCategory!=AdoIntegration&TestCategory!=ServiceNowIntegration". CI-LEARNINGS THAT BITE HERE: S4136 above all, and it breaks the build rather than the gate; CA1859 - the new test's helpers and locals take concrete types, and a local named for the port it exercises is the rule's exact target; NUnit2045 - the sequence assertion and any count assertion go in one scope, or collapse to one assertion; CA1861 - the expected sequence is a static readonly field, not an inline array inside Is.EqualTo; NUnit1028 - any TestCaseSource or helper is private static, and making it private brings CA1859 into scope in the same edit. COMMIT: refactor(feature-ordering) for the seam and the seeder, test(feature-ordering) for the new fixture - separate commits, because one is a change in structure and the other is a change in what is pinned. COMMENTS: IFeatureOrdering's doc-comment currently cites ADR-134 SA-2; rewrite it to say the thing itself - that this is the only production type that builds an ordering comparer, so every read path draws from one sequence rather than four that happen to agree. Never leave DDD-3, INV-A3 or ADR-187 section 4 in a comment.  NOTHING TO UN-IGNORE HERE: this step adds a new unit test rather than claiming a scaffolded acceptance scenario. Write it without a skip marker.

steps.name: One writer, and it decides the order of its own operations
criteria: Handing the order over gives every Feature a place, and the places follow the sequence the tracker gave rather than the order the rows were created in
Handing the order over and giving it back both re-queue the forecasts, through the shipped handler rather than through a spy on the bus
Giving the order back writes no places: a Feature that arrived while this instance owned the order still has none afterwards
Giving the order back and taking it over again returns the places this instance already chose, not a fresh reading of the tracker
Turning a setting that has no consequences on or off still just stores the value - the behaviour every row in the table has today is unchanged
Exactly one applier answers for each seeded setting: none is claimed twice, and none names a setting nobody seeds
The controller has no branch on which setting is being written
Faster Updates is still carried across untouched, and a write through the deprecated door still moves nobody
steps.implementation_notes: ONE METHOD, WHOLE WRITE. IOptionalFeatureApplier carries a Key and a single ApplyAsync taking the row and the new on/off value, and that method owns everything: any pre-write work, the Enabled change, the save, and any post-write publication, in that order. It is deliberately not a before/after pair of hooks - a two-phase hook can be called in the wrong order or half-called, and one method cannot. DefaultOptionalFeatureApplier sets and saves, which is what every row in the table does today. FeatureOrderingApplier seeds the missing places FIRST, then sets, then saves, then publishes FeatureOrderingPolicyChanged. THE SEED RUNS ON THE WAY OUT ONLY. The shipped write path seeds only when the value becomes manual, and that conditional is load-bearing rather than incidental: seeding on a disable hands out places nobody asked for and destroys the meaning of a null place, which is how the product records that a Feature arrived while the switch was off - and a null place is what makes taking the order over again append rather than renumber. Guard it on the new value, not on the old one. Publishing stays on BOTH transitions: a handler wired only to the enable path leaves an instance that gave the order back forecasting from an order it no longer uses. WHY THE SEED IS SYNCHRONOUS AND THE NOTIFICATION IS NOT: IDomainEventDispatcher swallows handler exceptions by design, which is right for metrics fan-out and wrong here - a dropped seed leaves an instance owning the order with every place null and nothing to say it failed. The forecast re-queue is genuinely a notification and can afford to be lost; the difference is worth one comment in the applier, written as the reason and not as a citation. OQ-2 IS DECIDED: A DICTIONARY BUILT FROM THE REGISTERED APPLIERS, not keyed DI. Three grounds, in order of weight. First, the enforcement rule ADR-187 names decides it on its own - the container exposes no inventory of its keys, so a keyed registration cannot be enumerated and exactly one applier per seeded key, no duplicates, no orphans would be unassertable; a rule that cannot be checked is a convention. Second, house style: keyed registration and keyed injection appear zero times across the backend, while the two shipped seams that pick from many implementations at runtime both enumerate the registered set - the database configurator enumerates every ISeeder, and the domain-event dispatcher enumerates every handler for the event. Third, cost is a wash - both are about ten lines - so the tie goes to the idiom already in the codebase. Inject the full set of appliers into a small OptionalFeatureApplierRegistry that indexes by Key at construction and falls back to the default for a key nothing claims. It must NOT be a switch: the work-tracking connector factory's switch on system type is the shape ADR-187 refuses here, because a key switch in or beside a controller is the five-if failure relocated one layer up. THE CONTROLLER resolves the row by key exactly as 02-01 left it, keeps its 404 and its 403 in that order, then asks the registry for an applier and calls it. It gains no if on which setting is being written; the premium check stays generic, reading the row's premium flag, so every premium row added after this one inherits the same answer without anyone deciding it again. THE STARTUP TEST THIS STEP OWES, from ADR-187's enforcement table: OptionalFeatureApplierSeamArchUnitTest in Lighthouse.Backend.Tests/Architecture/, following the naming and shape of the seam tests already there. Build the real host, run the seeders, read the seeded keys off the store, resolve every registered applier, and assert three things - no two appliers claim the same key, no applier names a key the seeders do not seed, and every seeded key resolves to exactly one applier through the registry. That last clause is what makes the default a deliberate fallback rather than an accident. Program.cs: register the two appliers and the registry beside the existing ordering-policy-provider and rank-seeder registrations. KEEP THE EDIT TO THOSE LINES: touching Program.cs puts this change on the shared-connector whitelist and forces the full backend Integration suite to run in CI, which raises live-connector flake exposure. That is unavoidable here and is not a reason to avoid the registration - it is a reason not to tidy anything else in that file while you are in it, and a reason to expect a longer, noisier CI run on this commit. WHAT GOES GREEN, AND THE ONE THAT DOES NOT: un-ignore The_places_are_seeded_in_the_order_the_admin_was_looking_at, Handing_the_order_over_and_giving_it_back_both_re_queue_the_forecasts, Giving_the_order_back_writes_no_places and Taking_the_order_over_again_restores_the_places_this_instance_already_chose. TWO OF THE FOUR ALSO PASS FOR FREE UNTIL YOU SABOTAGE THEM, so do that and watch each go red before committing: for Giving_the_order_back_writes_no_places, drop the condition and seed on every transition; for Taking_the_order_over_again, have the applier clear the places on disable. steps.name: One store behind both doors
criteria: Turning the ordering setting on for the first time leaves the Features list in exactly the sequence it was in a moment earlier, name and place together, on an instance where the tracker's ranking runs the opposite way to the row order
A write through the deprecated door is visible through the new one: the ordering row reads on, and the ordering read port agrees
An instance whose licence lapsed while it owned the order keeps it - its list does not change and the read path does not consult the licence
Turning it on through the deprecated door still moves nobody and still re-queues the forecasts once
There is exactly one way to write the ordering choice. Nothing outside the applier can change it, and nothing can change it without the places being seeded and the change announced
The ordering policy read port keeps its shape and its enum, and every consumer of it compiles and behaves unchanged
The deprecated write door still refuses an unlicensed administrator, by its own mechanism, exactly as it does today
The app setting the value was migrated from is still stored, and nothing reads it any more
steps.implementation_notes: THE STORE SWAPS BEHIND AN UNCHANGED INTERFACE. FeatureOrderingPolicyProvider takes the optional-feature repository instead of the app-setting one and maps the row's Enabled to the enum - true is ManualOrder, anything else including an absent row is SourceOrder, which is the same default an absent app setting has always meant. It stays the only place that knows the mapping exists, so ADR-132's reasoning survives at the level it was about: the enum is still the type every consumer sees, and anyone reaching for a bool in the ordering seam, the Features controller or the app-setting service is undoing it. DO NOT MAKE THE PROVIDER LICENCE-AWARE. It is the tempting tidy-up at exactly this moment, because the row it now reads is marked premium. It would hand every lapsed customer's list back to their tracker and reorder every Feature they had placed, silently, on their renewal date. An_instance_whose_licence_lapsed_keeps_the_order_it_already_owns is green today and is carried here as the guard against precisely that edit. SETPOLICY IS DELETED, NOT DELEGATED - that is this step's decision and the ADR must say so. Its sole caller moves to the applier, and a delegating SetPolicy would be a second name for a write the applier owns whole, which re-opens the two-entry-point shape the applier exists to close. Deleting it also leaves the ordering-policy port read-only, which is the honest shape: a port that only reads must not carry a method that writes, or the next caller will find it and use it. Remove SetPolicy from the interface and the implementation, and check the test doubles - grep the fully-qualified interface name as well as the short one, because a forgotten implementation in a test file is how this repository has broken its build before. AppSettingService.SetFeatureOrderingPolicy becomes a delegation to the applier for the ordering key: no seed of its own, no SetPolicy call, no second publish. AppSettingsController keeps both actions and the PUT keeps its premium licence guard - the 403 is then delivered on both doors by two independent mechanisms, which is what makes the alias safe to keep. AppSettingServiceTest has three tests that mock SetPolicy and SeedMissingRanks and assert the call order; they are asserting the mechanism that just moved, so rewrite them against the applier rather than deleting them - the ordering claim they make is still the claim worth pinning, only its owner changed. THE SCENARIO THAT FINALLY BECOMES DISCRIMINATING: Turning_the_ordering_setting_on_for_the_first_time_moves_nobody has passed since 02-02 and proved nothing, because the Features view was still reading its policy from the app setting. From this step the toggle actually changes what the view sorts by, and the assertion has teeth: the applier seeds the places from the tracker's sequence, the provider then reads ManualOrder, and the view sorts by places that reproduce the sequence it just showed. PROVE IT CAN FAIL: delete the seed call from the applier and re-run - with every place null and the policy reading manual, the tie falls to row id and the backwards-ranked fixture scrambles visibly. If it stays green under that sabotage, the fixture is not ranked backwards. A_write_through_the_deprecated_door_is_visible_through_the_new_one goes green here for the ordinary reason: both doors now write the same row. THE ADRs: amend ADR-187 with one line recording that SetPolicy was deleted rather than made to delegate, and why - DISTILL's obligation was to say which in the ADR, and an obligation discharged in a roadmap and not in the ADR leaves the next reader with the open question. Give ADR-134 the supersession banner naming ADR-187 for its section 1 and section A, and state explicitly that its sections 2, 3 and 4 and its enforcement rules are retained in full - a partially superseded ADR with no banner reads as current. GATES: dotnet build zero warnings under TreatWarningsAsErrors; dotnet test --filter "TestCategory!=Integration&TestCategory!=JiraIntegration&TestCategory!=LinearIntegration&TestCategory!=AdoIntegration&TestCategory!=ServiceNowIntegration". CI-LEARNINGS THAT BITE HERE: CA1859 - the provider's locals and any new private helper hold the concrete type, and a local named for the port it exercises is the rule's exact target; NUnit2045 in the rewritten AppSettingServiceTest, where the analyser does not see through a private assertion helper; CA1861 - the call-order sequence assertion needs a static readonly expected array, and ci-learnings records this exact test-strengthening moment as where inline arrays sneak in; S1192 and S125 as before. COMMIT: refactor(feature-ordering) for the re-backing and the deletion, test(feature-ordering) for the rewritten unit tests, docs(architecture) for the two ADR edits - three commits, because a store swap, a test rewrite and an architecture record are three different claims. COMMENTS: the ordering-policy port's doc-comment cites ADR-134 and must be rewritten to say what the port is for; AppSettingService.cs:101 opens with a D6 reference and that comment moves with the code it describes, rewritten as the reason itself - the places are read off the sequence the administrator was looking at, so they have to be taken before the choice is recorded. No D6, no DDD-10, no UI-6, no ADR-134 in any comment you leave behind.  UN-SKIP / UN-IGNORE, EXPLICITLY: remove the [Ignore] from Turning_the_ordering_setting_on_for_the_first_time_moves_nobody and from A_write_through_the_deprecated_door_is_visible_through_the_new_one. The first is the one that was vacuous until now - it can only fail once a seed exists to run in the wrong order, which is why it waited for the applier rather than going green at 02-02. The committed suite ships green - every scaffold carries a skip marker and DELIVER removes them one at a time. A step that implements the behaviour but leaves the marker in place turns nothing green and the suite still passes, which is indistinguishable from delivered work. Remove the marker, watch it fail, then make it pass.

steps.name: One heading, one table, nothing left behind
steps.scenario_name: puts every instance-wide switch under one heading
criteria: Settings then System shows one group named Behaviour Settings, and both instance-wide switches are rows in the table under it
No group named Optional Features and no group named for the Feature order remain anywhere on the page, and neither the standalone ordering switch nor its help text is rendered any more
The Features list still names its position column Manual while this instance owns the order and hash while the tracker does, and the label is derived from the setting the store now holds
The ordering switch is still disabled with the premium tooltip on an instance without the licence, and an unlicensed administrator still cannot reach the refusal from the page
Faster Updates still shows its preview badge and an enabled switch, and its row is unchanged
The end-to-end page object finds the table under its new heading, so the settings screenshot is taken rather than silently skipped
steps.implementation_notes: THE E2E TRAP, AND IT MUST BE FIXED IN THIS SAME CHANGE. SystemConfigurationPage.ts:183 locates the table with a getByText over the heading concatenated with the column names - Optional FeaturesNameDescriptionEnabled. Screenshots.spec.ts:106 guards the shot with an isVisible check on that locator. After the rename the locator matches nothing, isVisible returns false, and the screenshot is SILENTLY SKIPPED rather than failing: the docs image would never regenerate and nothing anywhere would say so. Move the locator to the new heading in the same commit as the rename. The other POM member is fine - enableFeature waits on a response whose URL merely contains /api/latest/optionalfeatures, which the keyed route still satisfies. THE RENAME: the InputGroup title becomes the literal Behaviour Settings. Keep the existing guard so the group renders only when there are rows; there always are now, but a page that renders an empty table on a fetch failure is a worse answer than one that renders nothing. THE DELETION: remove the whole InputGroup that wraps FeatureOrderingSettings, delete FeatureOrderingSettings.tsx and delete FeatureOrderingSettings.test.tsx with it - a test file for a deleted component either fails to compile or keeps a dead component alive, and neither is acceptable. Its label and its help text are not lost: they are the seeded name and description 02-02 put in the store, which is why the terminology work in 02-07 is owed rather than optional. THE HOOK READS THE SETTING NOW. useFeatureOrdering asks the optional-feature service for the ordering key and maps enabled to the policy, keeping its fallback to SourceOrder when the read throws or returns nothing - an instance that cannot answer follows its tracker, which is what it did before anyone could choose, and failing the other way would silently re-sequence every forecast. This is the design's recorded decision and it is worth being explicit about what it buys: the deprecated alias becomes genuinely inert on the client, which is what deprecated has to mean before it can ever be removed. It also means the boolean-to-enum mapping now exists on both stacks; keep the client's copy in this hook and nowhere else, because this hook is already the client's single ordering-policy read point and a second mapping is the frontend twin of the failure the seam on the server exists to prevent. Two hook test files arrange the old settings read and must be re-pointed at the optional-feature read: useFeatureOrdering.test.tsx and useFeatureOrdering.moveGate.test.tsx. Re-point them rather than leaving them - a test that mocks a call production no longer makes is green for a path nothing takes. OBLIGATION 6, THE POSITION COLUMN HEADING, IS DISCHARGED HERE AND NOT BY A NEW TEST. useFeatureOrdering.test.tsx already asserts the label is Manual when this instance owns the order and hash when the tracker does - one assertion per policy state, which is exactly what the obligation asks for - and FeatureListDataGrid.test.tsx already renders the column header for both label values with the hook mocked. Both halves of the chain exist; what this step owes is that the derivation half now runs off the store this story moved the value into, rather than off a service the hook has stopped calling. Leaving those two assertions pointed at the old read would have left the obligation formally satisfied and actually hollow, which is the failure mode worth naming out loud. WHAT MUST NOT REGRESS: shows the ordering switch as unavailable on an instance without the licence, never lets an unlicensed administrator reach the refusal, puts the switch back when the write is refused, changes nothing about the setting that was already in the list, and switches one setting without touching the other from 02-01. Also leaves a token nobody defined exactly where it is, which stays green here and stops being vacuous in 02-07. GATES: pnpm test; pnpm build with zero errors and zero warnings; pnpm biome check ./src clean - biome runs as the prebuild hook, so a clean build implies a clean check, but run it directly when only tests changed. Do not run biome with write enabled while docs symlinks are present in the tree. Do not commit a Playwright POM change you have not run against a live Lighthouse - the locator edit here is exactly the kind that passes review and matches nothing. COMMIT: feat(behaviour-settings) for the heading and the deletion, refactor(feature-ordering) for the hook rewire, test(behaviour-settings) for the re-pointed hook tests. COMMENTS: useFeatureOrdering's doc-comments cite AC-3.7, AC-3.8, AC-3.9, AC-3.10, ADR-134 SA-12 and ADR-136 SA-10. Every one of those names a section of a document a reader six months from now cannot resolve. Rewrite each as the reason it stands for - that four different reasons produce one visual state so they are decided in one place, and that an absent verdict from the server is not permission. Then remove the citations. WHAT GOES GREEN HERE, BY NAME: puts every instance-wide switch under one heading, and leaves no separate section behind. The second one is the reason the deletion and the rename are one step rather than two - it asserts the absence of the old group headings AND the absence of the standalone controls two testids, so a rename without the deletion passes half of it and a deletion without the rename passes the other half.  UN-SKIP / UN-IGNORE, EXPLICITLY: remove the it.skip from puts every instance-wide switch under one heading and from leaves no separate section behind. The committed suite ships green - every scaffold carries a skip marker and DELIVER removes them one at a time. A step that implements the behaviour but leaves the marker in place turns nothing green and the suite still passes, which is indistinguishable from delivered work. Remove the marker, watch it fail, then make it pass.

steps.name: The row reads in the instance's own word
steps.scenario_name: reads the row in the instance's own word for a Feature
criteria: An instance that calls a Feature something else reads its own word in the ordering row's name and in its description alike, and no placeholder is visible anywhere in the table
A token naming something the product does not have a term for is left standing exactly as written, braces and all
Every row and both cells get the same treatment - nothing is special-cased for the ordering row, and a row whose copy carries no token renders byte-identical to before
The resolver decides for itself whether a token names a real term, rather than asking the term lookup and accepting whatever it returns
The label an administrator read before this story on the standalone control is the label they read now in the table row
The server still stores and serves the token unresolved
steps.implementation_notes: ONE SMALL PURE FUNCTION, TWO CALL SITES. resolveTerms takes the text and the term lookup, walks the double-brace occurrences and substitutes only where the key is a member of TERMINOLOGY_KEYS; everything else is returned untouched, braces included. Syntax is double braces with camelCase keys - the features and feature keys are the ones this story uses - chosen because no seeded description contains a double brace today and single braces collide with ordinary prose. IT MUST CHECK MEMBERSHIP ITSELF. Delegating the unknown-token case to getTerm is the obvious shortcut and it fails quietly: getTerm returns the term's value, then its default, then the bare key, so an unknown key comes back as the key itself and a misspelled token would render as ordinary lowercase prose that survives review and ships. Dropping the token instead deletes a word from a sentence and reads as a bug in the copy rather than a bug in the copy's key. Leaving it visible, braces and all, is the only outcome a reviewer cannot miss. TERMINOLOGY_KEYS is a closed set on the client, so the membership check is a lookup and not a heuristic. THE NAME CELL IS IN SCOPE AND THAT IS NOT A WIDENING FOR ITS OWN SAKE. FeatureOrderingSettings.tsx:60 composed its label from the terminology lookup - the control's name was ALREADY terminology-aware in shipped code, while the table's name cell is a plain feature.name over a server-seeded string. 02-06 deleted that control. Resolving only the description would therefore not be declining to widen something new; it would ship a regression of behaviour users have today, which is exactly the objection this whole store was once rejected over. Apply the resolver to the name cell and to the description cell, for every row. DeltaSync's copy carries no token and must render byte-identical - the test that says so is green today and stays green. Write resolveTerms.test.ts alongside: a known token, an unknown token, several tokens in one string, a string with no token at all, and an empty string. PIN AT LEAST ONE USER-VISIBLE STRING AGAINST THE LITERAL rather than against the constant it came from - ci-learnings records self-satisfying assertions as the single most common surviving mutant in copy-bearing code, and blanking a constant to the empty string must not go unnoticed. THE VACUOUS TEST STOPS BEING VACUOUS: leaves a token nobody defined exactly where it is has passed since DISTILL because nothing resolved anything. From this step it is the only thing standing between a typo in seeded copy and a silently deleted word, so run it before and after and satisfy yourself it would fail if the membership check were dropped - sabotage the resolver to substitute unconditionally and watch it go red. RESOLUTION IS FRONTEND-ONLY. Nothing on the server changes here. The seeder stores the token because the term map is a client-side concern and the seeding path has no principal to resolve it for. GATES: pnpm test; pnpm build with zero errors and zero warnings; pnpm biome check ./src clean. CI-LEARNINGS THAT BITE HERE: prefer passing a single-argument pure function directly to map rather than wrapping it in an arrow; keep the resolver's branching well under cognitive-complexity fifteen, which one membership check and one replace comfortably is; use globalThis over window if either appears. COMMIT: feat(behaviour-settings). COMMENTS: at most one, on the membership check, saying why an unrecognised token is left standing rather than resolved or dropped - a reviewer has to be able to see a typo. Do not write AC-01.11, OQ-1, DDD-8, UI-3 or ADR-187 section 7 in it.  UN-SKIP / UN-IGNORE, EXPLICITLY: remove the it.skip from reads the row in the instances own word for a Feature. Also note that leaves a token nobody defined exactly where it is is already un-skipped and green, but vacuously so until this step ships the resolver - from here it is the only thing between a typo in seeded copy and a silently deleted word. The committed suite ships green - every scaffold carries a skip marker and DELIVER removes them one at a time. A step that implements the behaviour but leaves the marker in place turns nothing green and the suite still passes, which is indistinguishable from delivered work. Remove the marker, watch it fail, then make it pass.

steps.name: The docs say what the page now says
criteria: The configuration page documents one group named Behaviour Settings, and the ordering setting is documented as a row in that table rather than as a section of its own
What the ordering setting does, including what turning it back off keeps, is preserved in full - nothing an administrator relied on reading disappears in the fold
Every deep link elsewhere in the docs that pointed at the old section resolves to where the content now lives
The settings screenshot shows the new heading with both rows, and the file was actually regenerated rather than kept
The documentation uses the instance-configurable words for a Feature and a Work Item as the product seeds them, and never a word from one tracker's vocabulary
The asset keeps its filename and its path
steps.implementation_notes: THE HEADING AND THE FOLD: configuration.md:62 is the Optional Features heading and becomes Behaviour Settings. configuration.md:90 is Feature Order (Premium) with a Turning it back off subsection beneath it; that content folds in as the ordering row's entry under the new heading, beside the Faster Updates entry. Fold, do not summarise - the paragraph about turning it back off keeping the places you chose is the part administrators actually rely on, and it is the same promise the seeded description now carries in the product. THE ANCHOR BREAKS AND THREE PAGES DEEP-LINK IT. The generated anchor for the old section is linked from portfolios/detail.md:60, concepts/howlighthouseforecasts.md:122 and features/features.md:30. Renaming the heading changes that anchor and every one of those becomes a link into nothing. Grep for the anchor across docs/ and repoint each hit at where the content now lives; a broken deep link in published docs is not caught by any gate here. Note that concepts/concepts.md, concepts/worktrackingsystems/azuredevops.md, csv.md, jira.md and linear.md also contain a line reading Feature Order after a hash - check each before touching it, because those are query and CSV examples where a leading hash is data rather than a heading, and editing one would corrupt an example a user copies. THE SCREENSHOT, AND THE TWO WAYS IT SILENTLY DOES NOT REGENERATE. First, delete docs/assets/settings/optionalfeatures.png BEFORE the run: the regen keeps the OLD file when the pixel diff comes in under half a percent, and a heading rename with everything else unchanged is well inside that. Second, 02-06 moved the page object's locator to the new heading - if that edit was missed, the visibility guard is false and the screenshot spec skips the shot without failing, so confirm the file's modification time changed rather than trusting a green run. The run also needs a premium licence present or the ordering row renders disabled and greyed, which is not the picture the page is documenting; the licence fixture is gitignored and absent from every worktree, so import it from the main checkout first. Keep the filename and the path exactly as they are - the marketing website hot-links docs assets from main through a CDN, so a rename or a move breaks a page in another repository with nothing here to warn you. TERMINOLOGY: the prose uses the seeded defaults - Feature, Features, Work Item, Work Items - never Epic, Initiative or Story, which name a heading a Jira or Linear reader never sees. Where the docs describe the row's copy, describe it in those defaults and say that an instance which renamed the term reads its own word, because that is now true and is the thing this slice made true. GATES: no build gate applies to a docs-only change, but the screenshot run does - the screenshot spec must pass rather than skip, and its per-theme shape stays as it is. Run it locally; never commit a spec or a POM change you have not run against a live Lighthouse. NO SILENT N/A: every item on this list gets an explicit answer, including N/A with its reason. COMMIT: docs(behaviour-settings) for the prose and the links, and the regenerated asset with the prose it illustrates. COMMENTS: not applicable to Markdown, but the same rule governs the prose - do not write AC-01.11 or ADR-187 in a page a user reads. THIS STEP CLAIMS NO ACCEPTANCE SCENARIO. Its evidence is the regenerated image and the rendered docs page, checked by eye against the running page.

steps.name: The tests are worth what the slice claims
criteria: Both stacks are mutation-tested over the code this slice changed, and both clear the eighty percent kill rate
The result is recorded under the feature's mutation folder with the score, the command, the config used and the survivor judgements
The predicate that resolves a setting by its key is no longer uncovered - the mutant that inverts it is killed
Every surviving mutant is judged and written down: either a test is added that pins the behaviour, or the reason it is unkillable is stated
Every scenario this slice claimed is un-ignored and green, and no scenario the slice did not claim was edited
The whole suite is green under the standard filter, and the frontend suite, build and lint are clean
steps.implementation_notes: RE-ANCHOR THE CONFIGS BEFORE TRUSTING ANY NUMBER. The per-feature Stryker configs are gitignored, so nothing is inherited from slice 01 and every fix has to be made again. Stryker.NET ignores line ranges and whole-file mutate globs alike, so target files explicitly and expect the whole file's score rather than the changed lines'; where a file is large enough that its own neighbourhood buries the slice, recover the changed-lines figure by intersecting the report with git diff and say in the write-up which figure is the gate. Backend surface for this slice: OptionalFeaturesController.cs, OptionalFeatureSeeder.cs, FeatureOrderingPolicyProvider.cs, FeatureRankSeeder.cs, FeatureOrdering.cs and the three new applier files. Frontend surface: resolveTerms.ts, SystemSettingsTab.tsx, useFeatureOrdering.ts, OptionalFeatureService.ts. THE FRONTEND RUNNER HAS AN EXPLICIT INCLUDE LIST and SystemSettingsTab.behaviourSettings.test.tsx is a new file. If it is not in the stryker vitest config's include, every mutant in the code it covers survives for want of a test run rather than for want of a test, and the report cannot be told apart from a real gap. Add it before the first run, not after reading a bad score. StrykerJS has also been observed leaving type-checking suppressions in hundreds of files after a run - check the working tree is clean before committing. THE UNCOVERED PREDICATE FROM SLICE 01 IS THIS STEP'S TO CONFIRM CLOSED. OptionalFeaturesController.cs:25, the key comparison inside GetOptionalFeatureByKey, was NoCoverage because the unit tests mock GetByPredicate and Moq never invokes the lambda. 02-01 added The_setting_a_caller_names_is_the_setting_it_gets_back against the real repository to close it, and 02-06 made the client's ordering read depend on that endpoint. Verify the inverted-comparison mutant is now killed. If it is not, the scenario is not reaching the predicate and the finding is still open - report that rather than adjusting the config until the number looks right. JUDGE SURVIVORS, DO NOT JUST COUNT THEM. An equivalent mutant with no observable behaviour difference gets its reason written down; a survivor with behaviour behind it gets a test. The two places to expect real survivors are the migration branch in the seeder, where the three stored values are already parametrized and should leave little standing, and the applier's seed condition, where a mutant that seeds on both transitions must die on Giving_the_order_back_writes_no_places. If it survives, that scenario is not discriminating and the fixture needs the Feature that arrives after the first enable, which is the only shape that can tell the two behaviours apart. WHEN MUTATION-DRIVEN STRENGTHENING ADDS TESTS, RE-GREP THE FILES YOU TOUCHED: ci-learnings records this as exactly when CA1861 inline expected-arrays and NUnit2045 assert-pairs get in, both of which are invisible to dotnet build and fail only the Sonar new-violations gate. Also grep any new Try-shaped call for CA1806, and any new test file that touches JSON for a per-call serializer-options allocation. THE LEDGER ENTRY: append a slice-02 section to mutation/results.md in the shape slice 01 used - a score table per stack, the config and command actually run, the survivor judgements, and an explicit statement for anything reported N/A rather than a silent omission. Slice 01's frontend row reads N/A because it changed no frontend file; slice 02 changed several, so a frontend number is owed. BEFORE COMMITTING: confirm every one of the fifteen scenarios this slice claimed is un-ignored, and that Slice01PremiumRefusalTest and every scenario carried as a regression criterion are green. Do not run the backend suite while anything else is writing to the build output - a concurrent build poisons a run in flight and produces dozens of failures across unrelated subsystems, which is the tell. Expect the full Integration suite in CI on the Program.cs commit from 02-04, with the higher live-connector flake exposure that brings. GATES: dotnet build zero warnings under TreatWarningsAsErrors; dotnet test --filter "TestCategory!=Integration&TestCategory!=JiraIntegration&TestCategory!=LinearIntegration&TestCategory!=AdoIntegration&TestCategory!=ServiceNowIntegration"; pnpm test; pnpm build; pnpm biome check ./src. COMMIT: test(behaviour-settings) for any strengthening, docs(behaviour-settings) for the recorded run. COMMENTS: none are owed by this step, and any added while strengthening obey the same rule - no internal references, write the reason itself. THIS STEP CLAIMS NO ACCEPTANCE SCENARIO. Giving_the_order_back_writes_no_places is named above as the test that must kill the seed-on-both-transitions mutant; it is claimed and turned green by 02-04, not here.
